Best Time to Visit Seoul: Month-by-Month Weather Guide

⏱ 7 min read · 📅 September 30, 2026

The Ultimate Guide to Timing Your Seoul Adventure

Seoul is a city defined by its dramatic seasonal shifts, where high-tech skyscrapers and ancient palaces are framed by ever-changing natural backdrops. From the delicate pink hues of April to the crisp, golden canopies of October, each month dictates a different rhythm of life in the South Korean capital. Choosing the right time to visit isn’t just about checking a thermometer; it is about deciding whether you want to navigate the high-energy crowds of cherry blossom season or enjoy the quiet, snowy solitude of a Joseon-era palace in mid-winter. For the discerning traveler, understanding these nuances is the difference between a good trip and a transformative one.

Strategically, the city operates in three distinct phases: the peak seasons of spring and autumn, the humid monsoon summer, and the bone-chilling but budget-friendly winter. In terms of cost, a night at a luxury hotel in Myeongdong might run ₩350,000 ($260) during the October foliage peak, whereas the same room could drop to ₩180,000 ($135) in the depths of January. Logistics also fluctuate; while the Seoul Subway system remains the world’s most efficient year-round, your willingness to walk between Line 4 stations will certainly depend on whether it’s 30°C or -10°C outside.

Spring Awakening: March to May

Spring in Seoul is a celebrated resurrection. March begins with a crisp chill, as temperatures hover between 0°C and 12°C (32–54’F), but by the time April arrives, the city is transformed into a pastel wonderland. This is arguably the most popular time for tourism, driven by the arrival of the beotkkot (cherry blossoms). However, travelers should be aware of 'Yellow Dust' (fine particulate matter) that can occasionally drift from the Gobi Desert, requiring the use of KF94 masks for sensitive individuals.

For the quintessential spring experience, head to Yeouido Hangang Park (Subway Line 5, Yeouinaru Station, Exit 2). During the Yeouido Cherry Blossom Festival, typically in early April, over 1,800 trees create a canopy of pink. While the park is free to enter, budget roughly ₩15,000 ($11) for street food like bindaetteok and strawberry skewers from the local stalls. Another must-visit is Gyeongbokgung Palace (Line 3, Gyeongbokgung Station, Exit 5), open 09:00–18:00 (closed Tuesdays). Entry is ₩3,000 ($2.25), but it is waived if you wear a traditional Hanbok, which can be rented nearby for approximately ₩20,000 ($15) for two hours.

May is often considered the 'Goldilocks' month—neither too hot nor too cold. It hosts the Lotus Lantern Festival (Yeondeunghoe), a UNESCO heritage event celebrating Buddha's Birthday. The grand parade through Jongno is free to watch and offers some of the most vibrant photographic opportunities in all of Asia. As demand peaks, booking your flights at least three months in advance is essential to avoid prices exceeding $1,200 for transpacific routes.

💡 Pro Tip: To avoid the crushing crowds at Yeouido, visit Seoul Forest (Bundang Line, Seoul Forest Station) instead. It offers similar cherry blossom views with a fraction of the foot traffic and plenty of space for a picnic.

The Summer Heat and Monsoon: June to August

June marks the beginning of the heat, with temperatures rising toward 28°C (82’F). By July and August, the city enters its monsoon phase, known as jangma. Rainfall can be torrential, averaging 316mm in July alone, and humidity frequently sits at a stifling 77%. While this might deter outdoor hikers, it is the prime season for indoor urban exploration. Seoul’s massive underground malls and museum complexes become air-conditioned sanctuaries.

The Starfield COEX Mall (Line 2, Samseong Station, Exits 5/6) is a summer lifesaver. Home to the stunning Starfield Library, it offers free entry and thousands of books under a soaring glass ceiling. For culture, the National Museum of Korea (Line 4/Gyeongui-Jungang, Ichon Station, Exit 2) is free to enter and offers a comprehensive look at 5,000 years of history. Expect to spend around ₩12,000 ($9) for a hearty lunch of naengmyeon (cold buckwheat noodles) in the museum cafeteria—the perfect meal for a humid day.

August is the hottest month, with highs of 30°C (86’F). This is peak domestic vacation time, so while international flights might be cheaper due to the rain, local attractions like Lotte World (Line 2/8, Jamsil Station, Exit 4) will be packed with school children. A one-day pass here costs roughly ₩62,000 ($46), but many travelers find discounts through online booking platforms. Evening walks along the Cheonggyecheon Stream provide a natural cooling effect, as the water temperature is often several degrees lower than the surrounding pavement.

Autumn Splendor: September to November

If you ask a local, they will likely tell you that October is the best time to visit. The air turns crisp, the humidity evaporates, and the city erupts in shades of crimson and gold. September is a transition month where temperatures cool to 16–26°C (61–79’F). By mid-October, the foliage begins its peak, starting in the mountains like Bukhansan National Park (Line 3, Gupabal Station, then Bus 704) and moving into the city center by early November.

For the best fall colors, visit the Changdeokgung Palace Secret Garden (Line 3, Anguk Station, Exit 3). Access to the 'Huwon' requires a guided tour booking, which is highly competitive. Tickets are ₩8,000 ($6) including palace entry and should be booked online exactly six days in advance at 10:00 AM KST. Another iconic spot is the Deoksugung Stone Wall Road, a free walking path lined with ginkgo trees that turn a brilliant neon yellow. It is one of the most romantic spots in the city and is particularly beautiful at sunset.

November offers a great balance of beauty and value. While the first two weeks still boast foliage, the crowds begin to thin as the temperature drops toward 3°C (37’F). Hotel prices start to stabilize, and you can often find boutique stays in Bukchon Hanok Village for under ₩200,000 ($150) per night, compared to the much higher rates in October. The air is dry and clear, making it the best time for photography from the N Seoul Tower observatory.

Winter Magic and Value: December to February

Winter in Seoul is for the hearty. Temperatures frequently plummet to -10°C (14’F), and the wind chill whipping off the Han River can be biting. However, for budget-conscious travelers, this is the 'Golden Era.' Flight and hotel costs can drop by 50% compared to April. The city does not sleep during the cold; instead, it moves into jjimjilbangs (Korean bathhouses) and heated tents serving pojangmacha street food.

A visit to Dragon Hill Spa or similar large bathhouses typically costs ₩15,000 to ₩20,000 ($11–$15) for a 12-hour stay. It is the ultimate cultural immersion. For outdoor festive fun, the Seoul Plaza Ice Rink (Line 1/2, City Hall Station, Exit 5) opens in late December. Skating costs a mere ₩1,000 ($0.75) per hour, including skate rental, making it one of the cheapest activities in the city. Afterward, warm up with a bowl of galbitang (short rib soup) for about ₩18,000 ($13.50).

January is the coldest month, but it offers the lowest crowds at major landmarks. February remains chilly but sees the celebration of Seollal (Lunar New Year). During this three-day holiday, many shops close, but the major palaces host traditional folk games and performances. It is a unique time to see the city's traditional side, though travelers should avoid moving between cities as trains and buses sell out months in advance for the holiday exodus.

💡 Pro Tip: Buy 'Hot Packs' (chemical hand warmers) at any GS25 or CU convenience store for about ₩1,200 ($0.90). They last for 12 hours and are essential if you plan to walk through the outdoor markets of Namdaemun or Gwangjang in winter.

Essential Info & Quick Facts

  • Currency: South Korean Won (KRW, ₩). Current exchange is approx. ₩1,340 to $1 USD.
  • Connectivity: Rent a portable Wi-Fi 'egg' or buy a SIM card at Incheon Airport for roughly ₩35,000 ($26) for 10 days.
  • Transport: The T-Money card is essential. It costs ₩3,000 ($2.25) for the card, and a typical subway ride is ₩1,400 ($1.05).
  • Operating Hours: Most malls open 10:30–20:00; Palaces are generally closed on Mondays or Tuesdays.
  • Safety: Seoul is one of the safest cities globally, though 'Yellow Dust' masks are recommended in Spring.

Ultimately, there is no 'wrong' time to visit Seoul, only different versions of the city to discover. Whether you are chasing the ephemeral cherry blossoms or seeking the quiet, frozen beauty of a palace in January, Seoul remains a city of profound contrasts and endless hospitality. Pack your layers, bring your appetite, and prepare for a capital that truly has a season for everyone.
